title: A Lantern for the Absent
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
I couldn't decide what name to write on the lantern.

That was the trouble. There were names I remembered, names I had learned again, and names that lived just beyond my reach like objects at the bottom of dark water. If I wrote one, the others felt abandoned. If I wrote them all, I would have to admit how many empty spaces remained.

Mara watched me stare at the paper.

"You're allowed to leave it blank," she said.

"Everyone else is writing something."

"Everyone else is doing what they want."

She dipped her brush into a little pot of amber paint and continued a pattern of waves around her lantern. She had written nothing on it either.

"Who is yours for?" I asked.

"Somebody who hated being named in public."

I looked at her.

"Then why bring it?"

"Because I still want to carry a light."

That answer stayed with me.

Frostturn wasn't quite winter in Lanternweald. The weather didn't obey any one homeworld's calendar. The name belonged to a local stretch of short days, when the first hard frost reached the canal reeds and the western wind brought the smell of cold seaweed into Lanternwell Square. The Lantern Walk at Frostturn had once been a way for travelers to find their doors before night overtook the paths. Nowadays the district stewards still checked the crossings, but people also carried lights for memory, gratitude, mourning, or no reason at all.

Pip had painted signs showing the accessible route. Edda and Tamsin had marked the stretches where the cobbles were uneven. Danse had tested the pier lamps, and Iroh had insisted on hot tea for anyone who needed to stop along the way.

Nobody had to dedicate a lantern to anyone.

I knew this. I had helped write the notice.

Knowing wasn't the same as believing it for myself.

Maui swept toward the table carrying a basket of spare wicks and wearing a cloak with a fur collar so dramatic it could have belonged to a minor king. Someone had apparently told him the vigil wasn't a fashion event; he had treated that as a challenge. His grin eased when he saw my untouched lantern.

"I bring supplies," he announced, lifting the wicker basket like a trophy. "For what I assume is an extremely sophisticated lantern-making ceremony."

"It's paper and string."

"And bravery. Don't undersell bravery."

Mini Maui had somehow acquired an imaginary fur collar of his own. He strutted across the larger tattooed chest until Maui pressed a finger against the tiny figure and told it to behave.

I smiled despite the knot in my throat.

His expression softened a fraction. "Hey. I don't know who you're writing to. I don't have to."

"Good."

"But if you'd like company, my company is famously exceptional."

"And if I want to sit here without anyone talking?"

He looked aghast. "An unfair test of my greatest weakness."

I laughed. He sat anyway, made a show of sealing his lips, and lasted perhaps forty seconds before whispering that he'd defeated a storage cabinet that morning. Then he caught himself, shrugged, and pushed the basket toward me. I didn't need him to become silent or saintly. I needed him to recognize that the unnamed people I mourned were real, even when he couldn't put himself in their story.

"How many enemies have you defeated?" I asked.

"Today? None."

"Tragic."

"I did battle with a stubborn storage cabinet."

"Did you win?"

"It surrendered two hinges and a spider."

He put the basket down and looked at my blank lantern.

"Too many names?"

I nodded.

He didn't ask which ones.

He sat beside me and threaded a wick through a little brass ring. His injured hand had healed enough for ordinary work, though Fen still wouldn't let him touch the heaviest mooring ropes.

After a while he said, "I used to tell stories where everyone remembered me."

"That's not a surprise."

"No. But I thought if I made the story big enough, nobody would forget the people I'd lost along the way. I could keep them with me by talking."

"Did it work?"

"For a while. Then I realized some people wanted to be remembered quietly."

I ran my thumb over the paper.

"Some of mine might not even know I'm here."

"Do you want to go looking for them?"

"Someday. Maybe. Not because tonight tells me I have to."

He nodded.

I picked up the brush and painted a small circle in the center of the lantern. I left a gap at the top, an opening too small for a name but large enough for light.

"That's it?" Maui asked.

"For now."

"It's beautiful."

"You haven't seen it lit."

"I know what I like."

I smiled, then caught myself worrying that I had been unfair to him. He had listened to my grief so patiently, and I wasn't sure how to explain that loving him did not close the spaces I'd carried from before.

"Maui?"

"Hm?"

"Can I ask you something awkward?"

"I thrive on awkward questions."

"Do you?"

"Absolutely not. Ask anyway."

I put down the brush.

"You know I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory. I've told you that from the beginning, and I haven't changed my mind."

His expression remained open.

"I know."

"Sometimes I worry that when I miss people, you'll think I'm wishing you were someone else."

He looked at the lantern.

"I do wonder whether I'll be enough for the stories you haven't remembered."

"That's not a fair job to give you."

"I know." He hesitated. "But being a hero makes it very tempting to think every problem needs me."

I turned toward him.

"You don't need to replace anyone. You don't need to be the only person I love. I want you here because you're Maui, and because I choose you."

He let out a breath.

"And if you choose another person too?"

"Then I tell the truth. I don't expect you to agree to something just because it makes sense to me. We talk about boundaries, and you get to decide what you want."

He was quiet for a moment.

"I want to be someone you can come home to," he said. "Without making home a cage."

I reached for his hand.

"That's what I want too."

We stayed at the table until the lanterns were ready. Then Mara called for help, and the square became a pleasant disaster of people trying to carry hot drinks, spare wicks, and weatherproof coats at the same time.

Iroh arrived with a kettle. Greg had brought a small hand drum so people could keep pace without turning the walk into a concert. Toph tested the route by feeling the ground beneath her boots, and Aang helped the children hang lanterns where they could reach them safely.

Maui carried my lantern.

He didn't ask what it meant.

The procession began at Lanternwell. The bells rang once, soft and ordinary. Along the canal, the lights stretched into a line that seemed to float just above the water. Frost had caught in the reeds, making them shine at their edges.

I walked beside Maui past Jasmine Steps, then toward the cove.

A woman ahead of us stopped at a bench. She held a lantern painted with three small stars. Her face was wet. Nobody asked her to explain. Edda moved a cup of tea within reach, and the woman nodded her thanks.

It occurred to me that privacy could be a kind of hospitality. Not silence forced on someone who needed to speak, but room for the choice.

At the water, Maui lifted my lantern toward a hook beneath the signal post.

"Here?"

"Here."

He hung it carefully.

The flame caught the circle I'd painted, spilling light through the little gap.

For one terrible, beautiful moment I wanted to tell him every name. I wanted to invent the names I couldn't remember, if only to fill the absence.

Instead, I leaned against him and whispered, "I miss them."

"I know."

He didn't ask who.

I turned my face into his shoulder. His hand settled at the back of my coat, warm and steady.

"May I kiss you?" he asked quietly.

I nodded.

His lips met mine beneath the lantern, gentle enough that grief could remain in the room without being crowded out. I kissed him again because I wanted to, not because it made the night less sad.

Later we walked home after most of the lights had been extinguished. There were still several hanging along the safe route, each marked with a steward's name so no one would assume somebody else had put them out.

At our door, Maui paused.

"Do you want company?"

"Yes."

"And quiet?"

"Mostly."

"I can do mostly."

Fen came down the shore steps carrying the lantern tally, wick scissors, and a bent metal bracket.

"The west hook comes out of service until Tamsin checks the beam," Fen said.

Maui looked over. "I could fix that."

"You could hold the ladder while I remove it."

His expression suggested somebody had refused to applaud the sunrise. Mini Maui acted out a terrible fall from a miniature ladder, then crossed his arms in a tiny performance of outrage.

"You're supposed to be on my side," Maui told his tattoo.

Fen handed him the ladder. He planted its feet in the sand and kept them steady while Fen loosened the bracket. He didn't offer to pull the beam apart, replace the whole pier, or demonstrate how strong he was. I knew how much effort that took.

"The lantern list doesn't require names," Fen told me. "I only need to know which hooks are safe. Nobody checking the tally gets to decide whom you're missing."

When Fen left, Maui flexed his hands and gave me an injured look.

"Not one monster. Not a single heroic rescue. I was magnificent at standing still, and there's no audience."

"I was watching."

"Ah. My favorite audience."

The humor slipped from his face when he saw the blank space on my lantern. He didn't ask me to fill it.

"Do you want me here?" he asked.

I took his hand. "Yes. Not because you can hold a ladder."

"Good, because that ladder was vicious. Tried to stand upright the whole time."

I kissed him, and for a moment he seemed surprised enough to forget his next boast. The lantern remained unmarked, the bracket stayed off the rail, and the tide went on moving without asking us to explain our grief.

I laughed, tired and grateful. We sat with a blanket and a small bowl of warmed bread until the fire settled into coals.

The lantern at Tideglass burned until dawn.

It held no names.

It did not forget anyone.
